metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

extraction_notes.note: The ACE pseudocode is malformed: lines 2 and 3 both read 'Iterate until ... fails to decrease' (outer and inner loops) and the loop ends are printed as separate \STATE lines, so no nesting is syntactic. Kept lines as flat steps with loop subclass, dropped the two 'End ... Loop' lines.
The paper's findings are read off ACE transformation plots (figures not available as content); each stated observation was emitted as a numerical-rigor claim.
Corollary vs claim: the paper itself calls 'Shannon's theta^{-1} is bigger than Chernoff's' 'this corollary', so it is typed corollary although it is an inference from simulated plots.
The headline 'Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff' paragraph could be one remark; split into the claim sentence and the following physical/analogy argument as a heuristic proof.
MSC definition sentences introduce M, lambda_i and the per-symbol error together (one sentence lacks a space after its period); kept as one definition node.
Introduction restatements (mutual information, Chernoff information, the conjecture in the abstract/conclusion) and the PAC/SVM aside in Sec. 4.1 were not given separate nodes.

nodes.name: Data does not lie
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie.

nodes.name: PAC-style correctness with large probability
nodes.statement: For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].

nodes.name: Channel capacity
nodes.statement: As a matter of fact, the channel capacity is defined as maximization mutual information.

nodes.name: Mutual information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}].
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.genus: a measure of the amount of information
differentia: that one random variable contains about another variable

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: According to [\cite{Elements}], the Shannon mutual information is defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $X,Y$ are two random variables with marginal probability mass functions $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ and joint probability mass function $p(x,y)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.statement_short: $I_S(X,Y)=D(p(x,y)\|p(x)p(y))$, the KL divergence between joint and product of marginals.

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: Shannon Information

nodes.name: Relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler distance)
nodes.statement: The relative entropy is given by [\cite{Elements}]: \begin{equation} D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}} \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory

nodes.name: Relative entropy formula
nodes.statement: D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: KL distance

nodes.name: Chernoff information
nodes.statement: Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}]. As defined in [\cite{Elements}], it is given by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is real parameter with $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
differentia: when minimizing the overall probability of error
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff information $I_C(P_1,P_2)=-\min_{0\le\alpha\le1}\log\sum_x P_1^\alpha P_2^{1-\alpha}$, the optimal error exponent in hypothesis testing.

nodes.name: Chernoff information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: Chernoff Information1

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: With the aid of Chernoff information to describe the relationship between the two variables, a new mutual information is defined as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In this paper, we call it Chernoff mutual information relative to Shannon mutual information.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information: Chernoff information between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product $p(x)p(y)$.

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Chernoff Information2

nodes.name: Shannon vs Chernoff mutual information use different divergences
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].
nodes.statement_short: Both measures quantify dependence; Shannon uses relative entropy, Chernoff uses Renyi divergence.

nodes.name: Binary symmetric channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$.
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$

nodes.name: Transmission error $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $.

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: BSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: BSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: No closed form for BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is no explicit solution for Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}). As a result, it is arduous to analyze the Chernoff mutual information.\\ It is observed that the Shannon mutual information seems to be completely different from the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Multiple symmetric channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: M-ary symmetric channel with input probabilities $\lambda_i$ and per-symbol transmission error $\varepsilon/(M-1)$.

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: Predictors and response
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response.

nodes.name: ACE residual error
nodes.statement: Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables, the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalized squared residual of $\theta(Y)$ against $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$ for zero-mean transformations.

nodes.name: ACE residual error formula
nodes.statement: {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}}

nodes.name: ACE algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{ACE Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating conditional expectations: alternately update each $\phi_k$ by conditional expectation of the partial residual and renormalize $\theta(Y)$ until $e^2$ stops decreasing.
nodes.label: alg:ACE

nodes.name: Channel information as a function of channel parameters
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_p$ be the channel parameters and $Y$ be measured value of channel information. The functional relation between them is: \begin{equation} Y = f({X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Channel information $Y$ modelled as a function $f$ of channel parameters $X_1,\dots,X_p$.

nodes.name: Channel parameters known and independent
nodes.statement: It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent.

nodes.name: Channel information function known
nodes.statement: Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information.

nodes.name: ACE additive decomposition of channel information
nodes.statement: Therefore, it is easy to get $Y$ and they form a data set $\{Y,X_1,\cdots,X_p\}$. This data set meets the precondition of the ACE algorithm, so ACE algorithm can be used to analyze them. As a result, one can get \begin{equation} \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta \end{equation} where $\delta$ is residual error.
nodes.statement_short: The simulated data set satisfies ACE's precondition, so ACE yields $\theta(Y)=\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)+\delta$.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition
nodes.statement: \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta
nodes.label: ACE_Def

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \caption*{Simulation Procedure} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo: sample channel parameters, compute Shannon/Chernoff mutual information, and decompose with ACE, repeatedly.
nodes.label: alg:simulated

nodes.name: BSC simulation setup
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.
nodes.statement_short: 20000 samples of BSC Shannon and Chernoff mutual information with $\lambda,\varepsilon\sim U(0,1)$.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition quality for the BSC
nodes.statement: The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$. Furthermore, The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero. Clearly, both of them have shown that the ACE decomposition results are excellent.
conclusions: The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$.
The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero.

nodes.name: BSC transformations coincide for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is noted that function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition. As a result, in the range of the errors permitted, the $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ appears to be coincided with each other.
conclusions: function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition
nodes.statement_short: The ACE transformations $\phi_1(\lambda),\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ for Shannon and Chernoff mutual information nearly coincide on the BSC.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ for the BSC
nodes.statement: $\phi_1(\lambda)$ is monotone decreasing function. The greater $\lambda$, the faster the decline in $\phi_1(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Symmetry of $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ for the BSC
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is symmetric around the line $\varepsilon = 0.5$ for the fact that the channel is symmetrical about $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Shannon smaller than Chernoff on the BSC
nodes.statement: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical.
conclusions: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information

nodes.name: Shape of $\theta(y)$ for the BSC
nodes.statement: $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
conclusions: $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.

nodes.name: MSC simulation setup
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.
nodes.statement_short: 60000 samples of MSC Shannon and Chernoff mutual information with random $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition quality for the MSC
nodes.statement: Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I} shows similar characteristics that in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small. On the other hand, the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$. These two points verify the validity of the ACE algorithm again.
conclusions: The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small.
the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$.

nodes.name: MSC transformations coincide for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is obviously that the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures.
nodes.statement_short: On the MSC, all ACE transformations nearly coincide for Shannon and Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Shape of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ for the MSC
nodes.statement: It is worth noting that the minimum of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ occurs when $\varepsilon \approx 0.75$. The values of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is big when $\varepsilon$ is very close to $0$ or $1$.

nodes.name: Input-probability transformations alike for the MSC
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$ and $\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ are very similar. Their function curve is flat and close to zero when the independent variable (the probability of the input symbol) is less than $0.7$ . When the independent variable approaches to $1$, the values of them rapid decrease. In fact, it is reasonable because these input variables are equivalent for the channel.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$ are alike: flat near zero below 0.7, dropping rapidly near 1, as the inputs are equivalent.

nodes.name: Shannon smaller than Chernoff on the MSC
nodes.statement: As illustrated in Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical.
conclusions: the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information

nodes.name: Shape of $\theta(y)$ for the MSC
nodes.statement: $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is also close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.

nodes.name: ACE representation $Y=\psi(\varphi(\textbf{X}))$
nodes.statement: The ACE results is \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters.
assumptions: $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters
nodes.statement_short: Ignoring the residual, channel information is a composition $Y=\theta^{-1}(\sum_i\phi_i(X_i))=\psi(\varphi(\textbf{X}))$.

nodes.name: ACE results representation
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Res_Fun

nodes.name: Justification of equality (a)
nodes.statement: The equation ($a$) holds because the residual error $\delta$ can be ignored.
nodes.statement_short: Drop the ACE residual $\delta$ in the decomposition.

nodes.name: Inner function $\varphi$ shared by Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
conclusions: $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information
The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff share the same $\phi_i$ and hence the same inner $\varphi(\textbf{X})$; only $\theta$ (so $\psi$) differs.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $\theta$
nodes.statement: From the Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I} to Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function.

nodes.name: Argument for the corollary on $\theta^{-1}$
nodes.statement: As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information.
nodes.statement_short: From monotone $\theta$ with Shannon's values below Chernoff's, invert to compare $\theta^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ exceeds Chernoff's
nodes.statement: Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's.
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's

nodes.name: Corollary agrees with the data
nodes.statement: Actually, the facts extremely agree with the this corollary, which can well explain the phenomena in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC1 C and I}.

nodes.name: Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: In this sense, Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are different measures of the same channel information quantity.

nodes.name: Physical argument that Shannon and Chernoff measure the same quantity
nodes.statement: Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC. However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent. For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic: ACE reveals a shared structure; since channel parameters determine its state, both measures quantify the same thing, like kilometers and centimeters measure length.

nodes.name: Channel parameters decide the nature of the channel
nodes.statement: Obviously, the ability to convey information of a channel is decided by input parameters. That is to say, the parameters represent the channel. As a result, we hold opinion that these channel parameters decide the nature of channel.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: In this paper, we take $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ as the nature of channel information and we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the $\varPsi$ is the nature of channel information.
nodes.statement_short: The nature of channel information is $\varPsi=\varphi(\textbf{X})$, the inner ACE function of the channel parameters.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun

nodes.name: Channel information measures are functions of $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$, just as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information.
assumptions: $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information
conclusions: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$

nodes.name: Measure as function of nature
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun1

nodes.name: Information measures as compound functions
nodes.statement: As far as Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are concerned, their only difference is the function $\psi(\cdot)$. They can be seen as a compound function. The inner is $\varPsi$ which is the function w.r.t. channel parameters and the outer is the function w.r.t. $\varPsi$. For different channel information measures, the inner is always the same but the outer is different.
nodes.statement_short: Every channel information measure is $\psi(\varPsi)$: the inner $\varPsi$ is shared, only the outer $\psi$ varies by measure.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information conjecture
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent.
assumptions: a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent
nodes.statement_short: Any new channel information measure decomposes via ACE as some outer function $\psi$ of the shared nature $\varPsi$.

nodes.name: Uses of the conjecture
nodes.statement: This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$. In fact, even if this guess is not right with probability one, the new one which conforms to the law is correct with large probability and we can easily find the relation between that and previous information measures, such as Shannon and Chernoff information.
nodes.statement_short: The conjecture gives a test of a new measure's rationality and a recipe for designing measures via $\psi$.

nodes.name: Initialize
nodes.statement: set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;
nodes.statement_short: Set $\theta(Y)=Y/\|Y\|$ and all $\phi_k=0$.

nodes.name: Outer iteration
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;
nodes.statement_short: Outer loop: repeat until $e^2$ fails to decrease.

nodes.name: Inner iteration
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;
nodes.statement_short: Inner loop: repeat until $e^2$ fails to decrease.

nodes.name: Backfit each $\phi_k$
nodes.statement: For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;
nodes.statement_short: For each $k$, replace $\phi_k$ by the conditional expectation of the partial residual given $X_k$.

nodes.name: Update $\theta$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\theta(Y)$ by the normalized conditional expectation of $\sum_i\phi_i$ given $Y$.

nodes.name: Return solution
nodes.statement: $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;

nodes.name: Generate channel parameters
nodes.statement: Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$;

nodes.name: Compute information measures
nodes.statement: Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information;

nodes.name: ACE decomposition
nodes.statement: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm;

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeat above process till the required times.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the generation, computation and decomposition the required number of times.

nodes.name: Classical view
nodes.statement: Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the classical view: KL is the $\alpha=1$ case of Renyi divergence and the measures look different.

nodes.name: ACE reveals inner relation
nodes.statement: However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity.
nodes.statement_short: ACE decomposition shows they measure the same physical quantity.

nodes.name: Parameters determine the channel
nodes.statement: For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Channel parameters determine its state, so its information is consistent.

nodes.name: Units analogy and conclusion
nodes.statement: For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.
nodes.statement_short: By analogy with kilometers and centimeters, conclude both are metrics of the same quantity.
